scenes.text: This is EKYATRA Saathi.

Cancer care in India sits in a handful of cities. Most patients don't. A family from Gaya travels a thousand kilometres, nearly two days, to reach a hospital in Mumbai, and makes that journey again and again.
When a doctor takes leave, a scanner breaks, or a report runs late, the hospital knows. The family already on the train does not. Nobody's job is the space between the hospital and the home.
For a cancer patient, a wasted journey means money borrowed, wages lost, and a dose that slips. Long treatment is exactly where families drop out.

Saathi joins everyone a cancer journey runs through into one network: hospitals and labs, pharmacies, rail, bus and cabs, places to stay, equipment for care at home, and the scheme desks that pay. And it puts the family at the centre.
Each hospital is registered with its centres, doctors, and the machines patients depend on.
Then forty partners across eleven kinds: stays, rail and bus, cabs, labs, pharmacies, equipment, ambulances and insurers.
One form adds a partner: what it offers, which districts and hospitals it serves, how it answers, and who to fall back on if it can't.
A vendor can also apply on its own. A car service in Gaya, with no account, says what it covers, offers and charges.

It lands in the directory switched off, so nothing can route to it. A person reviews everything it said, including its prices, and approves. Five per cent commission, capped at eight, taken from our side: the family pays the vendor's own price.
Each hospital sets the rules the agents work inside.
Everything plugs in over open standards. Partners see dates and party size, never the diagnosis or the budget.
Taking a family on asks only what the family knows: who travels, and what they agree to share. Consent is recorded, and can be withdrawn.
The family app speaks five languages, reads aloud, and listens.
This is OpenEMR, a real open source hospital system, completely unmodified. Nothing of ours is installed in it. Saathi reads it over FHIR, and writes approved bookings back the same way.
The Control Centre sees every appointment, leave and machine, live.

Behind this is a team of agents doing the routine work: one watches the hospital, one reads what families say, one plans, one checks readiness, one finds rooms and bargains, and one checks every message before it goes. Two things always belong to a person: agreeing what a family meant, and approving any change to a booking.
The desk sees only what needs a person.

The network board puts every journey against every party: lab, report, scheme desk, pharmacy, slot, doctor, ride and stay. One family's cab firm said it can't go ahead, so Saathi has already found another way, and the plan waits for a person to approve it.
The long leg is the train: the right stations, straight to IRCTC. The last leg is routed live, with a time to leave.
One tap opens Google Maps, Gaya to the hospital door.
Another opens IRCTC to book.
Stays open in MakeMyTrip, with the hospital address copied.
Medicines in PharmEasy or Tata one M G. Rides in Ola or Uber. Nothing about the family goes with the tap.
Near the hospital: the cheapest bed first, then pharmacies and labs.
Every rupee is an estimate with its source, from railway fare slabs to meter tariffs. What the family tells us always wins.
The family logs a spend in their own words: a train ticket, seven hundred and eighty rupees.
It counts only once they confirm. Saathi then suggests help, like the railway's cancer concession.
They set a monthly limit only they can see. Overrun, and the hospital hears only to call.
The hospital tracks every report window, and who needs a person.
Now, live. A doctor marks Sunday as leave, an ordinary save in OpenEMR's own calendar. The appointments don't move, so anything watching only appointments sees nothing.
Saathi sees it within seconds, works out which families it hits, and asks each one, in their own language: which days work, who is coming, and what it costs them.
Kamla's family answers in Hindi: after the first, two of us, about fourteen hundred rupees.
An agent reads that into constraints. But before the planner may act, a navigator checks the reading against the family's own sentence.
The planner searches only the dates that fit what they said, and shows its working: every step, which agent took it, which needed a person, and every record it was built from.
One change, every family it touched.

The hospital caused this change, so the desk covers the extra cost from the patient welfare fund. Saathi shows why, the clinician was away, and roughly what it will cost, from published rates. One tick, one approval.
And the booking is written back into OpenEMR.
The family hears it in Hindi, with an apology: no extra cost to you.

scenes.chapter: A room, and a better rate
scenes.text: The new date needs a night in Mumbai, so an agent has already asked a rest house near the hospital for a room, and asks the family once: shall I ask for a better rate? On yes, it bargains. Two rounds at most, never above the first price, sharing only the dates and party size. A patient rate, breakfast included, and nothing is booked until the family taps.

The same change means different things to different families. Meera's dose moves three days earlier. Josephine's visit waits for her report. Arun lives close, so it costs him an afternoon. And Priya's three trips become one.

For doctors, a register of molecular tests already done. OpenEMR has no genomics resource at all, so Saathi keeps the fact of a test, never its result, and only with consent asked for that purpose alone.

Which test, which lab, who ordered it, and where the report is. A report that can't be fetched from here is flagged, before a repeat panel costing twenty-five to eighty thousand rupees. And type a finding into the note, and the server refuses it.
Every step is on the record, hash-chained, including the refusals and every offer in the negotiation. And every fact says where it came from.
With consent, journeys become research, without a name or an ID.
The hospital system runs the hospital. Saathi runs the patient's journey between hospitals, and plugs into any of them.
